methods.description: Identify circumference and diameter of the same circle; when radius is supplied double it, then divide the measured lengths and round the quotient. The measurement estimate is not exactly pi.
Use the same C/d constant for circles of different sizes; compare measurement quotients with pi to recognise a clearly inaccurate measurement.
Write C/d, explain why diameter lengths fit just over three times, and distinguish the reciprocal and C/r from pi.
Use the source decimal3.14159... and ordinary rounding to state the requested decimal approximation, keeping pi exact.

review.theoryObservation: Independently read the complete current intro/five facts and all 26 full solution fields, all four method definitions and every hash-bound mapping. Pi is exact C/d for the same circle, independent of size; measurements give estimates close to pi, not exactly 3.14. Radius doubling and the reciprocal/C/r contrasts use the actual definition and accepted circle-feature prerequisite. Rounding known pi is distinct from calculating a measurement estimate, explicitly demonstrated by q1 = 3.15. M2 correctly states C/r = 2pi approximately 6.28. There are no Theory.steps in either baseline or current theory, no changed procedural headers and no conflicting artificial bold stage labels. E0 teaches measured division/radius conversion; E1 teaches size invariance and a clear outlier; multipart E2 teaches definition/diameter-length interpretation and requested rounding. These cover every assigned method without unused quota labels. E0 unequal measurement roles expose division; repeated close estimates are the concept. E1 standard 22/7 is paired with 59.7/19 and the purposeful 3.60 outlier, rather than an incidental shortcut. All baseline diagram length readings use explicit labels, not unstated scale assumptions; no changed diagram field or new visual flag is needed.
